units.text: The ⟦0⟧,⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧ commands can be followed by a label (typically a single letter). Labels are defined with a colon followed by one or more letters (e.g. ‘⟦3⟧’). If the label is omitted the branch commands restart the cycle. Note the difference between branching to a label and restarting the cycle: when a cycle is restarted, ⟦4⟧ first prints the current content of the pattern space, then reads the next input line into the pattern space; Jumping to a label (even if it is at the beginning of the program) does not print the pattern space and does not read the next input line.
units.sourceHTML: The b,t and T commands can be followed by a label (typically a single letter). Labels are defined with a colon followed by one or more letters (e.g. ‘:x’). If the label is omitted the branch commands restart the cycle. Note the difference between branching to a label and restarting the cycle: when a cycle is restarted, sed first prints the current content of the pattern space, then reads the next input line into the pattern space; Jumping to a label (even if it is at the beginning of the program) does not print the pattern space and does not read the next input line.

units.text: Branching is often complemented with the ⟦0⟧ or ⟦1⟧ commands: both commands read the next input line into the pattern space without waiting for the cycle to restart. Before reading the next input line, ⟦2⟧ prints the current pattern space then empties it, while ⟦3⟧ appends a newline and the next input line to the pattern space.
units.sourceHTML: Branching is often complemented with the n or N commands: both commands read the next input line into the pattern space without waiting for the cycle to restart. Before reading the next input line, n prints the current pattern space then empties it, while N appends a newline and the next input line to the pattern space.

units.text: Both examples do not inf-loop, despite never starting a new cycle.
units.sourceHTML: • Both examples do not inf-loop, despite never starting a new cycle.

units.text: In the first example, the ⟦0⟧ commands first prints the content of the pattern space, empties the pattern space then reads the next input line.
units.sourceHTML: • In the first example, the n commands first prints the content of the pattern space, empties the pattern space then reads the next input line.

units.text: In the second example, the ⟦0⟧ commands appends the next input line to the pattern space (with a newline). Lines are accumulated in the pattern space until there are no more input lines to read, then the ⟦1⟧ command terminates the ⟦2⟧ program. When the program terminates, the end-of-cycle actions are performed, and the entire pattern space is printed.
units.sourceHTML: • In the second example, the N commands appends the next input line to the pattern space (with a newline). Lines are accumulated in the pattern space until there are no more input lines to read, then the N command terminates the sed program. When the program terminates, the end-of-cycle actions are performed, and the entire pattern space is printed.

units.text: The second example requires GNU ⟦0⟧, because it uses the non-POSIX-standard behavior of ⟦1⟧. See the “⟦2⟧ command on the last line” paragraph in ⟦3⟧Reporting Bugs⟦4⟧.
units.sourceHTML: • The second example requires GNU sed, because it uses the non-POSIX-standard behavior of N. See the “N command on the last line” paragraph in Reporting Bugs.

units.text: To further examine the difference between the two examples, try the following commands: ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧⟦2⟧⟦3⟧⟦4⟧

' aa bb cc dd | sed ':x ; n ; = ; bx'
printf '%s
' aa bb cc dd | sed ':x ; N ; = ; bx'
printf '%s
' aa bb cc dd | sed ':x ; n ; s/
/***/ ; bx'

' aa bb cc dd | sed ':x ; N ; s/
/***/ ; bx'
